subject: biology

items.q: Why is the wall of a capillary only one cell thick?
items.correct: It keeps the distance over which substances diffuse between blood and tissue cells very short.
items.misconception: It lets blood pass through the capillary faster, so that more blood reaches the tissue cells.
items.why: In everyday experience a thin-walled pipe is a light, easy-flow pipe, and students carry that intuition over. They have also learned that surface area and thin surfaces matter for exchange without connecting thinness to diffusion distance rather than to flow. A thin wall does not speed the flow of blood; in fact blood moves more slowly in capillaries than anywhere else. The wall is one endothelial cell thick to minimize the distance substances diffuse between plasma and tissue cells, which is what makes exchange rapid.
items.specStatementText: Capillaries are built for exchange
items.random_wrong: It leaves room for a lumen wide enough for red blood cells to pass through side by side.

items.q: A muscle receives blood through a network of thousands of capillaries rather than through a single vessel of the same total volume. What is the advantage of this arrangement for exchange?
items.correct: The total surface area of the many narrow, branching vessels is far larger, and all the blood is close to a wall.
items.misconception: A single wide vessel would have more wall area than thousands of narrow ones, so exchange inside it would be faster.
items.why: A single wide vessel obviously has a bigger wall than a single narrow one. Students compare one vessel with one vessel and do not think about the total surface area of the whole network, or about surface area in relation to the volume of blood inside. Capillaries are adapted for exchange by branching repeatedly and having narrow diameters. Splitting the blood among very many narrow vessels multiplies the total wall area and brings every red blood cell within a few micrometres of the wall, which is not true in a wide vessel.
items.specStatementText: Capillaries are built for exchange
items.random_wrong: The narrow capillaries force the blood through faster, so more oxygen is delivered to the muscle each second.

items.q: A micrograph shows two blood vessels in transverse section. Vessel X has a wall about as thick as the diameter of its small, round lumen. Vessel Y has a wall that is very thin compared with its wide, irregular lumen. Which identification is correct?
items.correct: X is an artery, because its wall is thick relative to its lumen to withstand high pressure.
items.misconception: Y is an artery, because its wide lumen carries the large volume of blood that is at high pressure.
items.why: Students associate high pressure with a large pipe, and know arteries are important vessels, so they expect the artery to be the larger, more open vessel in the section. In fact the high pressure is what allows an artery to have a relatively narrow lumen. In section the artery is recognized by the thickness of its wall relative to its lumen: the wall of muscle and elastic tissue is thick and the lumen is small and round. The vein has a much thinner wall and a lumen that is wide and often irregular in shape, because the low-pressure vessel wall collapses when it is cut.
items.specStatementText: Telling arteries from veins in a micrograph
items.random_wrong: X is a vein, because a vein needs a thick muscular wall to pump blood back towards the heart.

items.q: What is the role of the elastic tissue in the wall of an artery?
items.correct: It stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure.
items.misconception: It contracts in waves behind the blood to push it along the artery towards the tissues.
items.why: Muscle in everyday use means something that moves things, and students have met peristalsis, where muscular walls do push contents along a tube. They apply the same model to the muscular wall of an artery. Blood is propelled by contraction of the ventricles. The layers of muscle and elastic tissue in the artery wall allow it to withstand the high pressure produced and to maintain that pressure between beats; the muscle also narrows or widens the lumen to regulate flow, but it does not pump.
items.specStatementText: How arteries handle high pressure
items.random_wrong: It makes the wall stiff and rigid so that the high pressure cannot burst the artery.

items.q: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Which statement about this vessel is correct?
items.correct: It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, whatever the oxygen content.
items.misconception: It carries oxygenated blood, because by definition every artery carries oxygenated blood.
items.why: Diagrams colour arteries red and veins blue, and in the systemic circulation the rule happens to hold, so students turn a colour convention into a definition and forget the pulmonary vessels. Arteries are adapted for transporting blood away from the heart at high pressure, whatever its oxygen content. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart and the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood to it.
items.specStatementText: How arteries handle high pressure
items.random_wrong: Its wall is thick and rigid so that pressure from the right ventricle cannot burst it.

items.q: A student counts 12 beats in 10 seconds at the radial pulse. Immediately afterwards a digital heart rate monitor on the same person reads 74 beats per minute. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
items.correct: The values agree within the error of a 10-second count, about 6 beats per minute; a 60-second count would allow a fairer comparison.
items.misconception: The fingertip method gives 72 beats per minute but cannot be compared with the monitor, because it measures blood flow rather than heart rate.
items.why: The pulse feels like a throb of movement, and students are told that they are feeling the blood being pumped, so they take the sensation to be the flow of blood rather than a pressure wave in the wall. Blood flows continuously through the artery; what the fingertips detect is the wall expanding as the pressure wave from each ventricular contraction passes. That is why the pulse rate equals the heart rate and why the pulse can be felt only in arteries, where the pressure wave exists.
items.specStatementText: Taking a pulse
items.random_wrong: The fingertip count of exactly 72 beats per minute is precise, so the digital monitor must be reading 2 beats per minute too high.

items.q: Why can heart rate be determined by feeling the carotid or radial pulse with the fingertips?
items.correct: Because a pressure wave passes along the artery wall each time the left ventricle contracts.
items.misconception: Because these are the places where large veins close to the surface of the skin carry the heartbeat.
items.why: Veins are the vessels students can actually see under the skin, and they know the heart pumps all of the blood, so they expect the beat to be detectable wherever a vessel is close to the surface. The pulse is only found in arteries. The carotid and radial pulses are felt where an artery runs close to the skin. Blood pressure falls steadily through the arterioles and capillaries, and in veins it is low and non-pulsatile, which is why veins need valves and muscle compression to return blood.
items.specStatementText: Taking a pulse
items.random_wrong: Because blood is pushed past the fingertips in one surge each time the muscular artery wall contracts.

items.q: Which combination of features adapts a vein for returning blood to the heart at low pressure?
items.correct: Valves that prevent backflow, and a flexible wall compressed by surrounding muscle.
items.misconception: A thick layer of muscle that contracts rhythmically, and a narrow lumen that keeps the pressure high.
items.why: Students learn about the muscular walls of arteries and assume veins must have the same equipment to do the return journey, especially since blood has to travel upwards from the legs. Veins have only a thin layer of muscle and elastic tissue; their walls are thin and flexible precisely so that they can be squeezed flat by the skeletal muscles around them. Each squeeze pushes blood along, and the valves stop it flowing back when the muscle relaxes.
items.specStatementText: How veins get blood back
items.random_wrong: Valves that open and shut actively to push blood along, and a wall of elastic tissue that recoils.

items.q: A soldier standing motionless on parade for a long time feels faint, but the feeling passes as soon as she flexes her leg muscles. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: Standing still removes the muscle contractions that squeeze the leg veins, so less blood returns to the heart until she moves.
items.misconception: Standing still stops the valves in the leg veins from opening and shutting, so they no longer push blood up to the heart.
items.why: Because the valves are the feature always named when venous return is explained, students assign them the active role and picture them flapping to propel blood, rather than seeing them as one-way gates that only prevent backflow. Valves in veins have no muscle and generate no force. They are pushed open by blood moving towards the heart and pushed shut by blood trying to move away from it. The force comes from muscle action compressing the vein and from the small residual pressure left after the capillaries.
items.specStatementText: How veins get blood back
items.random_wrong: Standing still tires the muscular walls of the leg veins, so they can no longer contract to pump blood up to the heart.

items.q: A blood clot completely occludes a branch of a coronary artery. What is the direct consequence?
items.correct: The region of cardiac muscle supplied by that branch is deprived of oxygen and its cells die.
items.misconception: Blood can no longer pass through the chambers of the heart, so the heart stops beating almost at once.
items.why: The heart is full of blood, so it seems obvious that the heart wall is fed by that blood. Students picture the coronary arteries as part of the route the blood takes through the heart rather than as a separate supply to the muscle. The wall of the heart is too thick to be supplied by diffusion from the chambers. The coronary arteries branch from the aorta and run over the heart to supply the cardiac muscle. If one is occluded, the region of muscle beyond the block is starved of oxygen and cells die: a myocardial infarction. Blood continues to flow through the chambers, but the damaged muscle may fail to pump it effectively.
items.specStatementText: Blocked coronary arteries, and what correlations can prove
items.random_wrong: Fat from the diet keeps building up on the surface of the clot until the artery bursts open.

items.q: In a study of 20 countries, the correlation coefficient between mean saturated fat intake and the death rate from coronary heart disease was +0.85. What can be concluded from this result alone?
items.correct: There is a strong positive correlation between the variables, but this does not prove that one causes the other.
items.misconception: Saturated fat in the diet is shown to cause coronary heart disease, because the coefficient is so close to +1, the maximum.
items.why: Everyday reasoning and news headlines treat "linked with" as meaning "causes", and in laboratory experiments students have only ever met variables that were deliberately manipulated, so a pattern in observational data feels like the same kind of evidence. Correlation coefficients quantify the strength of a relationship and allow it to be assessed, and a low or absent correlation can be evidence against a hypothesis. But even the strong correlation between saturated fat intake and coronary heart disease does not prove a causal link: countries or people with high fat intake may also differ in smoking, exercise, sugar intake or wealth.
items.specStatementText: Blocked coronary arteries, and what correlations can prove
items.random_wrong: The relationship is weak, because a correlation calculated from only 20 countries cannot be a strong one.

items.q: Researchers calculated correlation coefficients between the incidence of coronary heart disease and four factors: smoking (2000 people) +0.72, hours of exercise per week (500 people) -0.65, dietary fibre intake (3000 people) +0.08, and blood cholesterol (400 people) +0.61. Which factor shows the weakest relationship with coronary heart disease?
items.correct: Dietary fibre intake, because +0.08 is closest to zero, showing little or no correlation.
items.misconception: Hours of exercise per week, because a negative coefficient shows a weaker relationship than any positive one.
items.why: In everyday language negative means bad and a bigger number means more, so students read the sign as part of the size. Graphs of positive correlations are also the ones most often shown, so negative correlations feel unfamiliar. Correlation coefficients run from -1 to +1. A value near -1 is just as strong a relationship as a value near +1; it simply means one variable falls as the other rises. Strength is judged by how far the value is from zero, whichever the sign.
items.specStatementText: Blocked coronary arteries, and what correlations can prove
items.random_wrong: Blood cholesterol, because it was measured in the fewest people, so its relationship is the weakest.

items.q: What generates the force that draws water up the xylem from the roots to the leaves?
items.correct: Evaporation of water from leaf cell walls draws water out of the xylem, putting the water column under tension.
items.misconception: Cells in the root pump water into the base of the xylem, pushing the whole column up to the leaves.
items.why: Pumps push from below in everyday experience, roots are where water enters the plant, and students may have seen root pressure demonstrated by sap oozing from a cut stem, so they locate the driving force in the roots. Root pressure exists but is far too small to lift water to the top of a tree. Water is pulled, not pushed: transpiration from leaf cell walls draws water out of the xylem vessels, creating a tension that is transmitted down the continuous water column and draws water up from the roots.
items.specStatementText: Water is pulled up the xylem, not pushed
items.random_wrong: The living xylem cells use ATP from respiration to move water molecules upwards against gravity.

items.q: In a tall tree the column of water in the xylem is under considerable tension, yet it does not break into separate lengths with gaps between them. Which property of water explains this?
items.correct: Water molecules are held to one another by hydrogen bonds, so the whole column moves as an unbroken unit.
items.misconception: Water molecules are attracted to the lignin of the vessel wall, which holds each part of the column in place.
items.why: Cohesion and adhesion are similar-sounding words met together, and students who picture water clinging to the vessel wall assign that idea to whichever word they remember. The everyday sense of sticking also suggests sticking to a surface. Cohesion is water to water; adhesion is water to the wall. Adhesion contributes to capillary action through cell walls, but it is cohesion, through hydrogen bonds, that ensures a continuous unbroken column of water in the xylem under tension.
items.specStatementText: Water is pulled up the xylem, not pushed
items.random_wrong: Water is pushed steadily upwards from the roots, so the column is kept under compression, not tension.

items.q: Why are the walls of xylem vessels thickened with lignin?
items.correct: To withstand the tension in the water column so that the vessel is not pulled inwards and collapsed.
items.misconception: To seal the vessel completely so that no water can escape through the side walls into surrounding cells.
items.why: Students learn that lignin is waterproof and picture the vessel as a sealed pipe with an opening at each end, so they have no way to explain how water reaches the leaf cells from the xylem in a vein. Xylem vessels are not sealed pipes. Their lignified walls contain many pits, through which water enters and exits the vessel along its whole length. This is how water passes into leaf cells from the xylem and how it can bypass a blocked vessel by moving into a neighbouring one.
items.specStatementText: Xylem vessels are built for flow under tension
items.random_wrong: To provide the mitochondria and cytoplasm of the vessel with a surface on which to generate ATP for transport.

items.q: A xylem vessel in a leaf vein is blocked by an air bubble. Water still reaches the leaf cells beyond the blockage. Which feature of xylem makes this possible?
items.correct: Pits in the lignified walls let water pass sideways into a neighbouring vessel.
items.misconception: Living xylem cells actively transport water around the blockage using ATP from respiration.
items.why: Students learn that moving substances against a gradient or uphill requires energy from the cell, and water in a tree is clearly moving uphill, so they assume xylem must be doing active transport. Xylem vessels are adapted for transport precisely by lacking cell contents: there is no cytoplasm, nucleus or mitochondria, which leaves an empty tube for unimpeded flow. The energy that lifts water comes from the sun, which evaporates water from the leaves and creates the tension.
items.specStatementText: Xylem vessels are built for flow under tension
items.random_wrong: The lignified side walls are completely sealed, so water can only move through the open ends.

items.q: A student is drawing a plan diagram from a micrograph of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous stem. Which description matches what should be drawn?
items.correct: A ring of vascular bundles near the outside, each with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the epidermis, and cortex outside the ring.
items.misconception: A single central mass of vascular tissue, with xylem forming a star and phloem between its arms, surrounded by a wide cortex.
items.why: Students picture transport tissue as a central pipe, and they may have seen the root arrangement, where the vascular tissue is central, and assume the whole plant is the same. In a stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring near the outside. This is the pattern to look for when drawing a plan diagram from a stem micrograph; a central star of xylem indicates a root, not a stem.
items.specStatementText: Tissues in a stem section
items.random_wrong: A ring of vascular bundles near the outside, each with phloem towards the centre and xylem towards the epidermis, and pith in the middle.

items.q: In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous root, where are the xylem and the phloem found?
items.correct: At the centre of the root, with the xylem forming a star shape and groups of phloem between its arms.
items.misconception: In separate vascular bundles arranged in a ring near the outside of the root, in just the same way as in the stem.
items.why: The stem section is usually learned first, and vascular bundle becomes the general name for any xylem-plus-phloem tissue, so students expect to find bundles in a ring wherever they look. In a dicotyledonous root the vascular tissue is central, with xylem in a star shape and phloem between its arms, and there is no ring of separate bundles. A wide cortex of parenchyma surrounds it and the epidermis with root hairs forms the outside.
items.specStatementText: Tissues in a root section
items.random_wrong: At the centre of the root, with phloem forming a star shape and xylem in groups between its arms.

items.q: Blood pressure in a capillary is about 4.7 kPa at the arteriole end and about 1.3 kPa at the venule end. How do these values explain the release and reuptake of tissue fluid?
items.correct: At 4.7 kPa the pressure forces fluid out through the capillary wall; at 1.3 kPa it cannot, so tissue fluid drains back in.
items.misconception: Plasma diffuses out at the arteriole end because its concentration is higher there, and diffuses back in at the venule end where it is lower.
items.why: Almost every other movement of substances across a barrier that students have met is diffusion, osmosis or active transport, so they reach for one of those names. Bulk flow of fluid forced through pores by pressure is a new mechanism. Tissue fluid is formed by pressure filtration, not by diffusion or osmosis. Blood arriving from arterioles is at a high enough pressure to force fluid through the capillary wall. Osmosis actually opposes this, because the plasma proteins left behind draw water back in, which is one reason fluid returns at the low-pressure venule end.
items.specStatementText: Tissue fluid leaves and returns (HL)
items.random_wrong: The pressure at the two ends is effectively the same, so fluid must be pumped back into the capillary by the venule.

items.q: Samples of blood plasma and of tissue fluid from the same tissue were analysed. Both contained about 5 mmol per litre of glucose and similar concentrations of sodium ions, but plasma contained about 70 grams per litre of protein while tissue fluid contained only a small fraction of that amount. Which explanation of these results is correct?
items.correct: Pressure filtration lets water and small solutes through the capillary wall but retains the large plasma proteins.
items.misconception: Tissue fluid should have exactly the same composition as plasma, so the low protein value must be an error in the analysis.
items.why: Tissue fluid is described as being formed from plasma, and filtered plasma sounds like plasma, so students assume nothing is held back. They rarely see plasma proteins listed as a separate component of plasma at all. Pressure filtration works like a sieve: water and small dissolved molecules pass through the gaps in the capillary wall, but plasma proteins such as albumin, and all the blood cells, are retained. The lack of protein in tissue fluid is the main difference in composition, and it is also what draws fluid back into the capillary by osmosis.
items.specStatementText: Cells trade with tissue fluid, not blood (HL)
items.random_wrong: The cells of the tissue took the protein directly from the blood inside the capillaries before the tissue fluid formed.

items.q: Which statement describes how excess tissue fluid is drained and what happens to it?
items.correct: It enters lymph ducts through gaps in their thin walls, valves prevent backflow, and the lymph is returned to the blood.
items.misconception: It enters lymph ducts, which pump it along with their thick muscular walls to the kidneys, where it is excreted.
items.why: Students expect any vessel that moves fluid to be muscular and self-propelling. They have not seen that lymph ducts resemble veins, with thin walls, low pressure and valves, and that they depend on external compression. Lymph ducts have thin walls with gaps through which tissue fluid enters, and valves that prevent backflow. They are squeezed by surrounding muscle action, in the same way as veins, and the valves turn that squeezing into one-way flow back to the blood circulation.
items.specStatementText: Lymph drains the excess (HL)
items.random_wrong: It stays in the lymphatic system as lymph, a separate fluid that circulates without rejoining the blood.

items.q: In a bony fish, mean blood pressure was measured at about 5 kPa in the artery leaving the heart and about 3.5 kPa in the vessel leaving the gills. In a mammal, mean pressure in the aorta was about 13 kPa. What do these data show about the two types of circulation?
items.correct: In the fish, blood loses pressure in the gill capillaries and goes on to the body at that lower pressure; in the mammal it is pumped again after the lungs.
items.misconception: Both circulations are double, because in each case the blood passes through two capillary beds, one for gas exchange and one for the rest of the body.
items.why: Students learn that a double circulation has a lung circuit and a body circuit, and see that a fish has a gill circuit and a body circuit, so they count the two capillary beds rather than the number of passes through the heart. Single and double refer to how many times blood passes through the heart per circuit. In a fish the blood goes heart, gills, body, heart, passing through the heart once. In a mammal it goes heart, lungs, heart, body, heart, passing through twice.
items.specStatementText: Single and double circulation (HL)
items.random_wrong: The fish data must be unreliable, because blood leaves a capillary bed at the same pressure as it had when it entered, so the two fish values should be equal.

items.q: Which sequence correctly traces deoxygenated blood from the body through the heart and back to the body?
items.correct: Vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
items.misconception: Vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, right atrium, right ventricle and aorta
items.why: In a diagram of the heart in the frontal plane the right side of the heart appears on the left of the page, because it is drawn as if facing the viewer, so students who label from the page rather than from the body reverse the two sides. The heart is labelled from the owner's point of view, so the right atrium and right ventricle are on the left of a frontal-plane diagram. Blood flows vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta, and each step should be traced on the diagram with this in mind.
items.specStatementText: The heart delivers blood under pressure (HL)
items.random_wrong: Venae cavae, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary vein, lungs, pulmonary artery, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta

items.q: The wall of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. Which statement correctly explains this difference?
items.correct: The left ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to drive blood through the whole systemic circulation.
items.misconception: The left ventricle pumps a larger volume of blood at each beat than the right ventricle, so it needs more muscle.
items.why: A bigger, more muscular chamber suggests more blood to students, and the left ventricle is often described as the powerful side of the heart, which sounds like it does more work by moving more. Both ventricles pump the same volume of blood per beat; if they did not, blood would accumulate in one circuit. The difference is pressure: the thick cardiac muscle of the left ventricle generates the high pressure needed to drive blood around the body, while the thinner right ventricle produces the lower pressure appropriate for the delicate lung capillaries.
items.specStatementText: The heart delivers blood under pressure (HL)
items.random_wrong: The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, which offer more resistance to flow than the rest of the body does.

items.q: The sinoatrial node fires. Which sequence of events then follows in the left side of the heart?
items.correct: The atrium contracts, filling the ventricle; the ventricle then contracts, shutting the atrioventricular valve and opening the semilunar valve; then both relax.
items.misconception: The atrium and the ventricle contract at the same moment, and the atrioventricular and semilunar valves open together to let blood into the aorta.
items.why: A heartbeat is felt and heard as one event, and the heart is usually described as contracting or beating as a single organ, so students picture a single simultaneous squeeze. The impulse from the sinoatrial node spreads across the atria first, so atrial systole happens before the impulse reaches the ventricles. This sequence matters: if the ventricles contracted at the same time as the atria, they would not fill properly and the atrioventricular valves would close before the atria had emptied.
items.specStatementText: The cardiac cycle and blood pressure readings (HL)
items.random_wrong: Muscles attached to the valves pull them open one after the other, and the ventricle contracts only after both valves have been opened.

items.q: A person's blood pressure is recorded as 120/80 mm Hg. Which interpretation of the two values is correct?
items.correct: 120 is the arterial pressure at the peak of ventricular systole and 80 is the arterial pressure during ventricular diastole.
items.misconception: 120 is the pressure inside the left ventricle when it contracts and 80 is the pressure inside the left atrium when it relaxes.
items.why: Systole and diastole are learned as phases of the heart, so students assume the pressures named after them are measured inside the heart. They do not connect the cuff on the arm with an artery. A blood pressure measurement is taken in an artery, not in a chamber of the heart. Interpreting readings such as 120/80 mm Hg means recognizing the higher number as the arterial pressure produced when the left ventricle contracts and the lower number as the arterial pressure maintained by elastic recoil while it relaxes.
items.specStatementText: The cardiac cycle and blood pressure readings (HL)
items.random_wrong: 120 is the pressure during systole and 80 is the pressure the artery wall itself generates as it contracts to push blood.

items.q: A cut stem of a well-watered plant exudes sap from the xylem for several hours. When the roots are treated with a respiratory inhibitor, the exudation stops. What does this show about how the sap was being pushed out?
items.correct: Root cells were using ATP to pump mineral ions into the xylem, so water entered by osmosis and produced a positive pressure.
items.misconception: Root cells were actively transporting water into the xylem, and this active transport of water molecules needs ATP from respiration.
items.why: Students learn that root pressure involves active transport and that the result is water moving, so they conclude that water is what is actively transported. The idea that water is never actively transported but always follows a solute gradient by osmosis is easily lost. Water is not actively transported. Root pressure is generated by active transport of mineral ions into the xylem; the resulting osmotic movement of water into the xylem raises the pressure. This is why root pressure stops if the root is deprived of oxygen or treated with a respiratory inhibitor.
items.specStatementText: Root pressure pushes from below (HL)
items.random_wrong: The exudation was caused by tension pulling water up the xylem, and the inhibitor stopped the transpiration that generates it.

items.q: Droplets of water appear at the leaf tips of a grass seedling overnight, when the air is saturated with water vapour, but not during a dry, sunny day. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Humid air stops transpiration, so root pressure generated by active ion transport pushes water up and out of the leaf tips.
items.misconception: At night the roots generate a tension that pulls water up the plant and out of the leaf tips, taking over from the pull of transpiration.
items.why: Both are called pressures and both move water up the same tube, so students merge them into a single upward force. They have not noticed that one is a push generated at the bottom and the other a pull generated at the top, with opposite signs. Transpiration generates tension, a negative pressure potential, pulling from the leaves. Root pressure is the opposite: a positive pressure potential generated in the roots by osmotic uptake of water following active transport of ions. Root pressure can only move water when the pull from transpiration is small or absent, such as in high humidity or before the leaves open in spring.
items.specStatementText: Root pressure pushes from below (HL)
items.random_wrong: At night root cells use ATP to actively transport water molecules into the xylem, and this pumping of water forces it out of the leaf tips.

items.q: Which feature of a sieve tube element helps sap to flow along the phloem?
items.correct: It has lost its nucleus and most of its cytoplasm and organelles, so little inside it obstructs the sap.
items.misconception: It is dead and empty like a xylem vessel, so there is nothing inside the cell to slow the flow of sap.
items.why: Xylem and phloem are learned as a pair, xylem vessels are dead, and a cell with no nucleus sounds as if it cannot be alive, so students extend the xylem model to phloem. Sieve tube elements are living but highly reduced: they lose their nucleus, ribosomes and most organelles so that sap can flow freely, and the neighbouring companion cell, with its nucleus and many mitochondria, carries out the functions they cannot. Unlike xylem, phloem must be alive because loading of sap requires active transport.
items.specStatementText: Phloem: sieve tubes and companion cells (HL)
items.random_wrong: Its end walls are solid plates that hold the sap under pressure so that it flows faster along the tube.

items.q: In spring, sugars stored in the roots of a deciduous tree are converted to sucrose and carried in the phloem to the opening buds. Which statement about this transport is correct?
items.correct: Companion cells in the root use ATP to load sucrose into the sieve tubes, and the sap flows up to the buds, the sinks.
items.misconception: Mitochondria in the companion cells provide the ATP that physically drives the sap along the sieve tubes up to the buds.
items.why: Students learn that phloem transport is active and needs ATP, and that companion cells supply it, so they picture the energy being used to propel sap along the tube rather than to move sugar across a membrane at each end. ATP from the companion cells is spent on loading and unloading. Active loading of sugars at a source lowers the water potential in the sieve tube, water enters by osmosis and the resulting pressure drives the sap towards the sink, where unloading has the opposite effect. Movement along the tube is by bulk flow, not by mitochondria pushing.
items.specStatementText: Phloem: sieve tubes and companion cells (HL)
items.random_wrong: Sap cannot move upwards in the phloem, so the sugars must instead be carried up to the buds in the xylem.

items.q: What are fenestrations and where are they found?
items.correct: Pores through the endothelial cells of the capillary wall, present only in some capillaries where exchange must be particularly rapid, such as in the kidney glomerulus. They let water and small solutes pass but not blood cells.
items.misconception: All capillaries have fenestrations, and the holes are large enough for blood cells to squeeze out into the tissues.
items.why: The word suggests windows or holes, so students picture large openings and, because capillaries are described as leaky and white blood cells are known to leave capillaries, assume cells exit through the holes and that every capillary has them. Fenestrations are found only in some capillaries, where exchange needs to be particularly rapid. They are tiny pores through the cell, big enough for water and dissolved substances but not for cells. Continuous capillaries, such as those in muscle, have no fenestrations.
items.specStatementText: Capillaries are built for exchange
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does an artery wall contain elastic tissue rather than being thick and rigid?
items.correct: The elastic tissue stretches when blood is forced in during ventricular systole and recoils during diastole, which keeps blood pressure high and blood flowing between heartbeats.
items.misconception: A thick artery wall is rigid, like a strong pipe, so that it cannot burst under the high pressure.
items.why: Students know arteries withstand high pressure and reason that the safest way to resist pressure is to be stiff. They have not connected the elastic tissue to what happens to the pressure between one heartbeat and the next. Artery walls are thick but elastic, not rigid. Stretching during systole stores energy that is returned by recoil during diastole, which maintains pressure and smooths the flow so that blood keeps moving even while the ventricles are relaxed. A rigid wall would let the pressure fall to zero between beats.

items.q: Is a pulse count over 10 seconds multiplied by 6 as reliable as counting for a full minute?
items.correct: No. A miscount of one beat in 10 seconds becomes an error of 6 beats per minute after multiplying, whereas the same miscount in a 60-second count is an error of 1 beat per minute.
items.misconception: Counting for 10 seconds and multiplying by 6 gives exactly the same result as counting for 60 seconds, so the shorter count is just as accurate.
items.why: The multiplication is mathematically valid, so students assume the result is equally precise. They do not consider that any counting error or any beat that falls partly inside the interval is also multiplied by 6. Traditional pulse counting has an uncertainty of about one beat, and multiplying a short count scales that uncertainty up. Counting for longer, or repeating and averaging, reduces the error; this is one reason a digital heart rate monitor, which measures continuously, may give a slightly different value from a 10-second fingertip count.

items.q: Where does water actually evaporate during transpiration?
items.correct: From the wet cellulose cell walls of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces inside the leaf; the water vapour then diffuses out through the stomata.
items.misconception: Water evaporates straight out of the ends of the xylem vessels, or from the outer surface of the leaf, through the stomata.
items.why: Transpiration is often summarized as water loss through the stomata, and diagrams draw arrows from the xylem straight to the stoma, so students skip the step in which water moves through cell walls to the evaporating surface. Water leaves the xylem vessels through pits and moves by capillary action through the cellulose cell walls of the leaf cells. It evaporates from these cell walls into the leaf air spaces, and it is this evaporation that draws more water out of the xylem and generates tension.
items.specStatementText: Water is pulled up the xylem, not pushed
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why are the walls of xylem vessels lignified?
items.correct: So that they can withstand the tension in the water column without collapsing inwards; lignin also gives the plant support.
items.misconception: The lignin in xylem walls is only there to support the plant and hold it upright.
items.why: At GCSE and MYP level lignin is introduced as the strengthening material of xylem that supports the plant, and the idea that water under negative pressure would suck a soft-walled tube flat is new. Lignified walls do help support the plant, but for transport their key role is to withstand tension. The negative pressure potential in the xylem would collapse a thin-walled vessel, as sucking hard on a soft drinking straw collapses it; the rigid lignin prevents this.
items.specStatementText: Xylem vessels are built for flow under tension

items.q: In a vascular bundle of a dicotyledonous stem, which tissue lies nearer the centre of the stem?
items.correct: The xylem lies on the inner side of each bundle, towards the centre; the phloem lies on the outer side, towards the epidermis.
items.misconception: The phloem is on the inside of the vascular bundle and the xylem on the outside, or the two are mixed together with no fixed arrangement.
items.why: Students learn xylem and phloem as a pair of names and, without a plan diagram in mind, have no reason to remember which is inside. Some also reason that phloem should be central because sugars are more valuable and need protecting. In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles form a ring, and within each bundle the xylem is towards the centre and the phloem is towards the outside, with cambium between them. This is the arrangement students must be able to draw from a micrograph.

items.q: What is the function of the cortex in a stem or root?
items.correct: The cortex is packing and storage tissue made of parenchyma cells between the epidermis and the vascular tissue; it stores starch and, in a green stem, its outer cells may photosynthesize. It is not a transport tissue.
items.misconception: The cortex is part of the transport system and carries water and sugars, because it forms most of the section between the outside and the middle.
items.why: In a plan diagram the cortex is the largest region and lies between the surface, where water enters, and the vascular tissue, so students assume its job must be transport. The word is also unfamiliar and easily confused with vascular. The main functions to annotate on a plan diagram are: epidermis, protection and (in roots) absorption; cortex, storage and packing; xylem, transport of water and minerals and support; phloem, transport of sugars and amino acids. Water does cross the cortex of the root to reach the xylem, but the cortex is not a conducting tissue.

items.q: Why does tissue fluid drain back into the capillary at the venule end but not at the arteriole end?
items.correct: Because blood pressure falls along the capillary as fluid is lost and resistance is overcome, so at the venule end the hydrostatic pressure is too low to force fluid out and tissue fluid drains back into the capillary.
items.misconception: Blood pressure is the same all the way along a capillary, so tissue fluid must be pumped back in by the venule.
items.why: Students picture blood vessels as rigid pipes in which pressure is the same everywhere, so they cannot see why the two ends of the same capillary should behave differently and invent an extra pumping mechanism at the venule end. The formation of tissue fluid is promoted by the higher pressure of blood from arterioles; the lower pressure at the venule end allows tissue fluid to drain back into the capillary. There is no pump: the difference in pressure between the two ends is what reverses the direction of net fluid movement.
items.specStatementText: Tissue fluid leaves and returns (HL)

items.q: Do cells in a tissue take oxygen and glucose directly from the blood?
items.correct: No. Cells are bathed in tissue fluid and exchange substances with it: oxygen and glucose diffuse from the tissue fluid into cells, and carbon dioxide and other wastes diffuse out into the tissue fluid, which exchanges with the blood.
items.misconception: Each cell is in direct contact with a capillary and takes what it needs straight out of the blood.
items.why: The phrase blood carries oxygen to the cells suggests direct delivery, and diagrams often show a capillary touching a cell with arrows drawn from blood to cell, leaving out the tissue fluid in between. Most cells are not in contact with a capillary. Substances leave the blood into the tissue fluid, cross the tissue fluid, and only then enter cells; the exchange between cells and their environment is with tissue fluid, which is why its composition matters.
items.specStatementText: Cells trade with tissue fluid, not blood (HL)

items.q: What happens to lymph after it has drained from the tissues?
items.correct: It is returned to the blood circulation: lymph ducts join together and empty into veins near the heart, so the fluid and the small amount of protein it carries rejoin the plasma.
items.misconception: Lymph stays within the lymphatic system and is a separate fluid that never rejoins the blood.
items.why: The lymphatic system is taught as a separate system with its own vessels and its own name, and is often met in the context of immunity, so students see lymph as a fluid in a closed circuit of its own. The lymphatic system is a drainage system. Excess tissue fluid that does not return to the capillaries enters lymph ducts through gaps in their thin walls, is carried along past valves that prevent backflow, and is finally returned to the blood circulation. Without this return, fluid would accumulate in the tissues.
items.specStatementText: Lymph drains the excess (HL)

items.q: What happens to the pressure of the blood in a fish after it has passed through the gills?
items.correct: It falls considerably, because of the resistance of the narrow gill capillaries, and it is not restored before the blood continues to the body, so body tissues receive blood at low pressure and flow is slow.
items.misconception: Blood leaves the gills at the same pressure it had when it left the heart, so single and double circulations deliver blood to the body equally well.
items.why: Students treat pressure as a property set by the heart that stays fixed throughout the circuit, and they see the difference between the two circulations as being only about keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart. Passing through a capillary bed always causes a large drop in pressure. In the mammalian double circulation the blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is pumped a second time, so it reaches the body at high pressure. In the fish it does not, which limits the rate of delivery of oxygen to the tissues.

items.q: What opens and closes the valves of the heart?
items.correct: Differences in pressure on the two sides of each valve. The atrioventricular valves shut when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure; the semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and shut when it falls below.
items.misconception: The heart valves are opened and closed by muscles, or by nerve signals timed by the pacemaker.
items.why: The valves are described as opening and shutting at particular moments in the cycle, as if they were doors being operated, and the whole heart is known to be muscular, so students assume the valves are actively worked. Heart valves are passive flaps of tissue with no muscle of their own. They are pushed open or forced shut simply by the direction in which the pressure difference across them tends to move blood. Their timing follows automatically from the pressure changes of the cardiac cycle.
items.specStatementText: The heart delivers blood under pressure (HL)

items.q: What starts each heartbeat?
items.correct: The sinoatrial node, a group of specialized cardiac muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium, generates an electrical impulse spontaneously; nerves and hormones only adjust how fast it fires.
items.misconception: Each heartbeat is triggered by a nerve impulse sent from the brain, and the heart would stop if the nerves were cut.
items.why: Students learn that the brain controls the body and that skeletal muscle contracts only when a motor neuron fires, so they assume cardiac muscle must also wait for a nervous signal. Cardiac muscle is myogenic: the pacemaker in the right atrium initiates the beat by itself, which is why a heart can keep beating after removal from the body. The brain, via nerves and adrenaline, speeds up or slows down the pacemaker but does not initiate each beat.

items.q: Why is arterial blood pressure not zero while the ventricles are relaxed?
items.correct: Because the elastic walls of the arteries, stretched during systole, recoil during diastole and keep the blood under pressure; the diastolic reading, typically about 80 mm Hg, is this maintained pressure.
items.misconception: When the heart relaxes there is nothing pushing the blood, so the pressure in the arteries drops to zero between beats.
items.why: Students link pressure directly to the heart pushing, so no push means no pressure. They also see diastole described as the relaxation phase and assume relaxation applies to the blood as well as to the muscle. Diastolic pressure is the lowest arterial pressure in the cycle, but it is well above zero. The artery walls were stretched by the surge of blood during ventricular systole and their recoil squeezes the blood onwards while the ventricle refills. This is why a reading is quoted as two numbers, such as 120/80, and why 80 is not 0.

items.q: What is a sieve plate, and does it obstruct the flow of sap?
items.correct: A sieve plate is the perforated end wall between two sieve tube elements. Its pores allow sap to pass from one element to the next, so the sieve tube is a continuous pathway for flow.
items.misconception: Sieve plates are solid partitions between the phloem cells that block or filter the sap.
items.why: The word plate suggests something solid, and students who know that xylem vessels have their end walls removed assume phloem must be different by keeping its end walls intact as barriers. Sieve plates are perforated: the pores are what make the plate a sieve. Sap flows through them from element to element, and the reduced cytoplasm of each element leaves the pores and the lumen clear. The plates give the tube strength without blocking the flow.

items.q: In which direction does phloem sap flow?
items.correct: From a source, where carbon compounds are loaded, to a sink, where they are unloaded. Sources and sinks can be anywhere in the plant, so sap may flow up or down, and the direction can reverse with the season.
items.misconception: Phloem sap always flows downwards from the leaves to the roots, in the opposite direction to the xylem.
items.why: The summary xylem up, phloem down is a common memory aid, and photosynthesis in leaves feeding roots is the only example many students have met, so downward becomes the rule. Phloem sap flows from source to sink. In summer a leaf is a source and a root, fruit or growing shoot tip is a sink, so flow can be upwards to a fruit or bud as well as downwards. In spring a storage root becomes the source and the opening buds the sink, and flow is upwards.
items.specStatementText: Phloem: sieve tubes and companion cells (HL)

items.q: What causes a coronary artery to become occluded?
items.correct: Fatty deposits (atheroma) build up within the artery wall and narrow the lumen; if the deposit ruptures, a blood clot forms on it and can block the vessel completely.
items.misconception: Fat from the diet travels in the blood and sticks to the inside of the coronary artery, gradually clogging it like grease in a drainpipe.
items.why: The drainpipe image is used in public health messages and everyday talk, and it links neatly to the known correlation between fat intake and heart disease, so students take it as a literal description of the mechanism. Atheroma develops inside the wall of the artery, beneath the endothelium, not as fat sticking to the surface of the lumen. The plaque narrows the lumen and stiffens the wall, and a clot forming at a damaged plaque is what finally occludes the vessel. Diet is a risk factor, but it does not act by fat lining the pipe.

items.q: Does a correlation calculated from more people show a stronger relationship?
items.correct: No. The strength of the relationship is given by the correlation coefficient itself. A larger sample makes the coefficient a more reliable estimate, but it does not make the relationship stronger or weaker.
items.misconception: A correlation is strong if it was measured in a large number of people, and weak if the sample was small, so sample size is what shows the strength of a relationship.
items.why: Students are taught that repeating measurements and using large samples makes results more reliable, and reliable and strong blur together. In evaluating epidemiological data they therefore reach for the sample size as the measure of how convincing a relationship is. Correlation coefficients quantify the strength of the relationship between two variables on a scale from -1 to +1. Sample size affects how much confidence can be placed in that value, which is a separate question. Evaluating epidemiological data means considering both, but a coefficient of +0.08 shows a weak relationship however many people were studied.
